title: Run a team of up to 1,024 agents to rebuild a program
summary: Microsoft researchers had up to 1,024 coding agents rebuild programs like Pandoc with no boss agent; they report Pandoc's test pass rate rose from 34% to 55%.
agent_role: Agents claimed sub-tasks, shared findings, checked results and merged work on their own over six hours; humans set the goal and budget.
outcome: Researchers report the mean test pass rate across five hard tasks rose from 19.31% with 1 agent to 28.78% with 128 agents.
what_they_did: A Microsoft research team built a setup where many coding agents work as a team without a central boss. They share a code workspace and a chat channel. Each agent picks a piece of work, tries it, checks it and merges it. They asked teams to rebuild programs like Pandoc from their behavior and documentation, with six hours and no internet.
how_it_went: The authors report Pandoc's test pass rate rose from 33.89% with one agent to 55.06% with 1,024 agents. With a newer model, 32 agents reached 79.59% versus 56.19% for one.
worth_knowing: The team says roles like integrators and reviewers emerged on their own as teams grew. The public release is a single-machine setup for reproducing the experiments.
prompt: Help me set up a small team of coding agents to rebuild [program name] from its documentation and observed behavior. Plan how agents will claim sub-tasks, share progress in [shared repository] and a chat channel, and verify work against [test suite]. Start with [number] agents and a [time budget]. Show me the plan and the launch commands, and wait for my approval before starting any runs.

source.name: Hacker News
source.author: Zhihao Zhan et al. (Microsoft), posted by brunoborges

curation.rationale: A research release with code and numbers showing up to 1,024 coding agents rebuilding programs together; well evidenced but hard for most readers to reproduce.
